That sort of faith belongs only to the outward person. Mystics have criticised it as fides mortua, a dead faith. There may even be a deep and troubling connection between faith understood in this narrowly historical way, the rise of the view that everything must be explained through history, and the decline of philosophy. Ultimately, there may be a connection between the dominance of this historical faith and the preparation or arrival of what became known as historical materialism.

We have already recalled a teaching repeated by several Shiite Imams: if the revelations of the sacred Book had only this kind of “historical meaning,” the whole Book would have died long ago. More precisely, they give the phrase historical meaning an entirely different sense. For them, it does not mean an outward event locked away in the past, buried with the people who died, and now interesting only to archaeologists. It means something that is fulfilled again and again in living people, right up to the Last Day. It concerns the inward person and events that are entirely real, although they do not occur on the physical level of existence. This is the inner meaning of scripture, and its truth does not depend on outward historical circumstances.

Around this living meaning of the sacred Book, we find spiritual families coming together across different places and periods. On the Christian side, we would need to study the figures known as the Spirituals of Protestantism: Sebastian Franck, Valentin Weigel, and Caspar Schwenckfeld; the circles shaped by Jacob Boehme's teachings on divine wisdom, and later by Swedenborg's Arcana Caelestia; and thinkers such as Oetinger, together with the Christian Kabbalists, whose work cannot be separated from Jewish Kabbalah.

On the Islamic side, we would need a systematic account of how the Qur'an has been interpreted in search of its spiritual meaning. That story begins with the Imams themselves, continues through Ismaili and Twelver Shiite thought, and includes the great Qur'anic commentaries of sages and mystics such as Ruzbihan, Ibn Arabi, Semnani, Haydar Amoli, and Mulla Sadra Shirazi. It reaches as far as the Shaykhi school, which we will meet again in Chapters IV and V. So far, time has allowed me to make only a beginning on this kind of comparative study of spiritual interpretation.

If we pursued it more deeply, we would begin to see both what the worlds beyond our senses have in common and what their interpretation reveals about the inward human being. We would discover shared features of the inner traditions based on prophecy—and, unfortunately, shared features among their opponents, too. These may be religious lawyers and scholars of the Law, the fuqaha, or figures like the Grand Inquisitor portrayed by Dostoevsky.
We will meet their counterparts again when we consider the return of the Twelfth Imam in Book VII.

By learning to share this understanding of the sacred Book, we could begin to understand the problems we face together and find a language in which to address them. Earlier, I mentioned a small Shiite study circle in Tehran that I had the pleasure of joining, year after year, during my autumn visits. Its central figure was Shaykh Muhammad Husayn Tabataba'i, a professor of traditional philosophy at the theological university in Qom. The group also brought together some colleagues from Iran's new university, several religious teachers, and a number of their students who represented the traditional culture.

I repeatedly noticed how readily these friends understood the situations and questions arising from an inward reading of the Bible. Some passages by Meister Eckhart and Jacob Boehme, translated into Persian, and even episodes from our legends of the Holy Grail, seemed to speak a language very close to their own. The same could not be said of the ways we in the West try to explain our present situation. Our methods of argument, our social analysis, and our attempts to describe events in the language of cybernetics are not immediately accessible to Eastern friends who still have the privilege of living fully within their inherited culture.

More seriously, our way of viewing the present hardly seems to interest them. To them it is only natural that people should drift towards chaos after losing their spiritual centre—their “polar dimension”—and becoming unable to see any higher or vertical order except as a social relationship of power and domination. Our own questioning and protest are themselves called into question. And that is precisely where a shared problem may begin.
Westerners must accept responsibility for the consequences of a situation no one asked them to create. They must produce their own antidote to it.

But they can do so only if they understand what they have brought about, including disasters of the kind described in the moving testimony I will quote shortly. They must learn to value what they are in the process of destroying, and at last understand why those who remain its guardians value it so deeply.

Sometimes we face problems of translation that seem impossible to resolve. Words such as laicisation, secularisation, materialisation, socialisation, and evolutionism cannot simply be carried over into Persian or Arabic. We have to use longer explanations, give familiar words new meanings, or invent unfamiliar terms. Yet none of these methods produces in our Eastern listeners quite the same feelings and associations that those words awaken in us. This remains true even of friends who seem thoroughly “Westernised.”

The fact that we lack a shared vocabulary for our most urgent problems—and that it can be equally hard to translate the rich philosophical language of Shiite thinkers into our own languages—shows that we lack a common spiritual “past.” I do not mean shared outward events. I mean a shared experience of the inward person and the worlds of the soul: an experience that takes place in the soul's own time, the time of its unfolding story.

That story develops as the inner meanings of the sacred Book come alive within a person. It is not a one-way sequence of events that can never recur. We saw that the Imams refer to this story when they explain ta'wil, the practice of uncovering scripture's spiritual meaning. Western spiritual writers are speaking of the same kind of experience. In this time of the soul, we can bring about something that genuinely happens between us. A shared spiritual reading of the sacred Book can be its starting point.

Unfortunately, our own spiritual thinkers are still little known to these Eastern friends. What they have heard of Christianity comes largely from missionaries and defenders of the faith—or, more overwhelmingly, from the modern ideas that have spread out of post-Christian societies, turning older religious mysteries into worldly doctrines. The Christianity supposedly “driven out of history,” yet kept alive by our spiritual writers in the history of their own souls, remains almost unknown to them. When we introduce it, they welcome it warmly, as the examples above suggest.
But most people still fall back on the tired contrast between Western machines and technology on the one hand, and Eastern spiritual tradition on the other.

That is why I want to end these opening reflections by showing why we sometimes need to reverse this oversimplified contrast, particularly if we are to overcome the same dangers together. I shall set two striking testimonies side by side. The first comes from Nikolai Berdyaev, a representative of the Christian philosophy of Russian Orthodoxy. Our Eastern friends generally know little about that philosophy, although it is much closer to their thinking than our political and social ideologies are. Few people have protested more clearly than Berdyaev against the danger of allowing collective social life to swallow up the life of the spirit.
The second testimony comes from a Sunni Arab public figure. It shows the dead end to which an excessive drive to become Western can lead.

Berdyaev's fearless originality makes him impossible to place in any one school, apart from the tradition of divine wisdom associated with Jacob Boehme, to which he often explicitly declared his allegiance. His whole body of work develops the central theme of The Meaning of the Creative Act. It goes beyond an angry protest: it is a revolt against an age “in which sociological consciousness has replaced theology [...]. The domination of social life over modern consciousness weighs like a nightmare; this outward social world conceals and extinguishes every authentic reality.”

For, as he writes, “In every age, mysticism has discovered the world of the inward person and set it against the world of the outward person.” What mystical experience revealed was that the human being is a microcosm: a whole world in miniature. This is also one of the great themes of Islamic mystical wisdom.
Yet it is precisely what a purely social and supposedly scientific view of human life ignores or rejects. Such a view breaks the human being's connection with the cosmos.

And we should not confuse this connection with space travel. Today's rockets and satellites cannot restore what has been broken. There is a Threshold to cross, and no rocket or satellite can ever cross it. Once the connection is broken, all that remains is a rather pitiful individualism, helpless in the face of collective pressure and demands for conformity. The mystic, by contrast, carries a whole universe within and can stand in balance with the world outside.

This is the paradox of mystical experience: going deeply into oneself is also a liberation from oneself, a movement beyond one's boundaries. For “all mysticism teaches that the depths of the human being are more than human, that a mysterious bond with God and the world lies hidden there. It is within oneself that one finds the way beyond oneself.” The bonds that hold us are broken through an inward work, “from within and not from without.”

That conviction led Berdyaev to insist that “the human being studied by psychology is still only the outward person. The psychological is not the mystical. The inward person is spiritual, not merely psychological.” This distinction recalls the old Gnostic difference between those who live by the spirit and those who live only at the level of the soul. It is central to his thought, because it shapes how the mystic responds when living faith is turned into an external object, a system of beliefs.

“Religions,” he writes, “translate into knowledge and fixed forms of being what mysticism experiences and reveals directly. The dogmatic teaching of the universal Churches has been an objective translation of mystical experience as it was immediately lived [...]. Dogmas decline and die when they lose their mystical source, when they concern themselves with the outward person rather than the inward person, when the experience they express is physical and psychological rather than spiritual. Faith based on historical fact is the faith of the outward person, whose spirit has not reached down to the mystical sources. It is faith adapted to the physical level of existence.”

We can now understand why I suggested an unsettling connection between the demands of strictly historical faith and the coming of an age dominated by historical materialism. The same theme runs through Berdyaev's Essay in Eschatological Metaphysics. “Christ rejected the temptation of the kingdoms of this world in the desert, but in the course of history Christians yielded to that temptation.” For Berdyaev, this is what happened when Christianity directed towards the last things gave way to Christianity adapted to the conditions of external history.

From that point, the transformation of Christianity into something worldly had begun. We need to grasp this if we are to understand the secular forms of social messianism that appeared in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. We also need it to resist the claim that history possesses a fixed and unquestionable meaning. For such a meaning cannot be understood without a dimension beyond ordinary history—the “polar dimension” mentioned earlier, connecting human beings to a heavenly pole. And it is precisely this dimension that a strictly factual, socially focused view of the world removes from human awareness.

I have stressed this attempt to recover a mystical Christianity, oriented towards the final fulfilment of things, because Berdyaev's work suggests that Westerners may be able to produce an antidote to the damage done when Christianity is reduced to a social system. It is almost a kind of spiritual homeopathy. But what happens elsewhere, where the poison comes from outside and is therefore harder to recognise for what it is?

Islam, too, has always looked towards the final fulfilment of things, especially Shiite Islam. But can Islam now produce its own antidote to imported ideologies that are destroying the spiritual life it once possessed? This is the serious question already raised here, and it stands at the centre of the situation we must face together.

Consider, by contrast, the words of a prominent Muslim from Jordan, part of the Sunni Arab world. They were spoken in an interview some years ago, but I would not change a word, since the situation has, if anything, become more widespread and more severe. He said:

Because I live in the modern world and have received a Western education, I can imagine progress only outside tradition. Many of us in Jordan think this way and try to bring together things that cannot be reconciled. Like our Arab and Muslim brothers everywhere, when we begin to think seriously, we face a terrible inner conflict. Can we separate religion from a social system that scientific and technological progress has condemned, without killing God? In the Islam we know, religion and society are inseparable; neither exists without the other. Can we modernise without condemning ourselves to damnation?

What makes this testimony so painful is the way a person's whole inner life has been taken over by an ideology to which that person cannot find an antidote, because its basic assumptions come from elsewhere. Here is a Muslim who takes pride in a Western education.

Yet the Western influence visible in his words contains nothing of the resistance expressed by Berdyaev in the passages we have just read. Quite the opposite: it comes from precisely the ideologies Berdyaev was opposing.

The first revealing statement is the slogan “live with your times.” Who will help this bewildered Muslim discover the awareness and strength to live in his own time—not the time imposed by an anonymous collective, but his personal time, the time in which his own existence unfolds? This is the time in which a teaching becomes true and meaningful through his own living commitment to it, not because it belongs to some date in the historical past or to the social arrangements of an earlier age.

Yet Islamic spiritual thinkers explained this distinction beautifully. They spoke of outward, historical time (zaman afaqi) and the time of the soul (zaman anfosi). They knew that a tradition can be passed on alive only in this second kind of time, because there it remains a continually renewed inspiration, not a funeral procession or a register of approved opinions. The life and death of spiritual things are our responsibility. We make them “things of the past” only when we give up on them and refuse the changes in ourselves that would keep them alive in the present.

The task is not to attempt “impossible syntheses.” It is to understand what spiritual thinkers have always understood, expressed in the saying of Imam Ja'far recalled earlier: “Islam began as a stranger, and it will become a stranger again. Blessed are the strangers!”

For spiritual thinkers, the danger of damnation—the danger of “killing God”—has never chiefly lain in separating spiritual life from social life. Strangely enough, they have seen it in confusing religion with a particular social system and treating the two as one. The separation at stake is more radical than merely distinguishing “spiritual power” from “temporal power.” As we observed earlier, as long as we speak of power and authority, we have already begun to turn spiritual life into a social institution. We are already somewhere on the path leading to Nietzsche's cry, “God is dead.” And we have just heard an unexpected echo of that cry on the lips of a Muslim.

So, only a few weeks after the interview appeared, we put a question to ourselves in our small Shiite study circle in Tehran: what would a Shiite have to say? What would someone say who truly lived Islam as Din-e Qiyamat, the religion of Resurrection?

The interview might indeed describe the tragedy of any form of Islam identified entirely with sharia, the religion of religious law and outward practice. But what if sharia is understood as only one half of religion in its fullness? What if the other, essential half is haqiqa: spiritual truth, the saving knowledge that is itself Resurrection (Qiyamat)?

There are profound differences between Arab Islam and Iranian Islam. We need not explore them all here. One of them, however, is the spiritual outlook that, at the time I am writing, helps protect Iranian Islam from being drawn into political passions and extreme racial or national feeling. This is why the universal meaning of Islam as a religion, beyond the boundaries of nations, is experienced and expressed with particular clarity in a country such as Iran.

What is certain is that the Jordanian speaker makes no mention at all of the two sides of religion represented by sharia and haqiqa. His education has probably left him quite unaware of the distinction. On one side is religion understood as Law: left to itself, it becomes no more than a social religion. On the other is spiritual religion, religion lived in truth, whose substance is the spiritual meaning of divine revelation. This meaning does not depend on any particular social order.

Even during the most severe upheavals of public life, a believer can remain faithful to the requirements of sharia, because observing them is a personal matter between that person and God. But this remains possible in its full sense only when outward practice is kept alive by haqiqa, the inner truth. Where, then, does that inner truth come from? What is its source?

As we discussed the interview among friends in Tehran, we came to see that this question goes to the very heart of Shiite spiritual life. It led us back to the foundations of Shiite philosophy and religious experience. What matters most is the role played by its understanding of prophecy and of the Imams. Together, these place Shiism at an equal distance from two positions: a religion reduced to outward rules and legal requirements, and the implications of the Christian doctrine that God became incarnate.

Shiism presents itself instead as a “straight path” (sirat mustaqim). On one side lies an abstract, rigidly unified idea of one God. On the other lies the kind of doctrine associated with the Church and its authority, which can become a worldly ideology: the idea that the divine is embodied in society itself, once theology gives way to thinking about religion solely in social terms.

Equally important is ghayba: the concealment of the Imam, his present invisibility. The hidden Imam points to a divine presence that remains unrecognised, a spiritual community rather than an institution defined by worldly power, and an expectation directed towards the end of time: the Imam's return, or parousia.

This expectation gives meaning to humanity's present condition because it anticipates the condition's end in a transformation of heaven and earth. The very idea of the Imam's concealment rules out turning religion, in its deepest sense, into an institution or a social object. His return, which we will examine again in Book VII, is not simply an event that will arrive from outside on some future day.

The Imam is hidden because human beings have made themselves unable to see him. His future appearance presupposes a change in human hearts. Through the way his followers live and become who they are, they themselves have a part in bringing about that appearance. Until then, the period of the Great Occultation is the time of an unrecognised divine presence. Precisely because this presence remains hidden, it cannot be turned into an object, a thing, still less something that society can take possession of. The time of the hidden Imam is therefore not merely historical time. It is the time of lived existence.

The contrast can now be summed up. Shiite teachings about prophecy and the Imams resist attempts to turn spiritual life into a social system because walayat concerns spiritual initiation and inner knowledge, not the foundation of a Church. The Friends of God, the “people of God,” are guides who lead others into spiritual understanding. They are not an institution empowered to impose dogma.

Visions and manifestations of God through particular spiritual figures do not require the doctrine of an Incarnation in which the divine is brought into ordinary physical history. The Imam's concealment preserves the expectation of a final transformation, as it did in early Christianity. It also preserves a hidden spiritual community—an Ecclesia spiritualis—whose inner order cannot be captured by public institutions and therefore cannot be turned into a worldly one.

The correspondence between the cycle of prophecy and the cycle of walayat makes it possible to recognise a continuing sacred history: a history that unfolds in the spiritual world, rising from one level to another, rather than simply moving along the endless straight line of conventional historical progress. Truth does not depend on where we stand on a timeline. It depends on the height of the horizon from which we perceive it. The Great Occultation is not a period in which we “make history” in the outward sense. It is a form of lived time. The Hidden Imam is the time of Shiite consciousness itself, its continuing link with what lies beyond ordinary history.

These reflections help us see what kind of problems we need to overcome together. Earlier, I mentioned the paradox of Shiism's outward position, beginning with its own political success under the Safavid restoration in the sixteenth century.

We will return to it in Chapter II. The powerful work of Haydar Amoli in the fourteenth century, and of Mulla Sadra Shirazi and his students in the seventeenth, draws on the teaching of the Imams. Such thinkers can help Twelver Shiism confront its own paradox by recognising the present meaning of its spiritual message and of the struggle to remain faithful to that message (see Chapter III).

Let me close this chapter with one striking observation. Twenty years ago, it was unusual to meet a young Iranian intellectual with whom I could discuss the philosophy of Mulla Sadra Shirazi. At the time I am writing, that is no longer exceptional. This is not something that will ever interest statisticians, but something is beginning to take shape. The pages of this book hope to contribute to it, however modestly.
Of course, I know that many Iranians, young and old alike, are deeply committed to the teachings of the great spiritual masters discussed here.

But others, also of every age, have grown used to dismissing these names and ideas. For some, the dismissal springs from ignorance; for others, refusal often hides a longing for what they have lost. I hope this book will at least give them the courage to acknowledge that longing. There is no reason to surrender to the myth of the inevitable “direction of history,” a myth that cannot see as living in the present what it calls the past, because it imagines it has already left that past behind.

We recalled earlier the Imams' teaching that the inward meaning of divine revelation is its true historical meaning. That is because its inward meaning never stops unfolding in the inward person, right up to the Last Day. In this sense, spiritual meaning is historical meaning: it belongs to the history of the soul, and that history keeps it alive in the present.

This is why tradition, by handing on what it protects, creates something new each time—not fashionable new ideologies, but new witnesses. That is certainly different from the usual idea that history belongs to the past.

But is this way of understanding things in the present really less honest or rigorous than the supposedly new methods of historical research? When archaeology, economics, and sociology are used to present the past lives of anonymous masses as the true “subject of history,” are we not still looking into a mirror? Is it not our own assumptions, preferences, and resentments that shape the image we read there in the present—all, of course, in the name of objectivity?

There is an image I am particularly fond of, one that I will return to here. It came to me as I contemplated the dry riverbeds that cut across the high Iranian plateau. Often, in the company of these same friends, we imagined the unforeseeable day when living water would once again fill those channels to the brim.

Then we would ask ourselves: where does the future of a living stream lie, whether it is a river of this world or a stream of spiritual life? At the mouth where the ocean swallows it? In the sandy desert where it disappears? Or at its source? Might its source be its true future?

For when we speak of the life of the soul, past and future are not properties of external things. They belong to the soul itself. It is we who are alive or dead, and we who are responsible for the life or death of these things. That is the secret of the Imams' way of uncovering scripture's spiritual meaning.

Mulla Sadra, for example, understood very well that we know only as much as we love, and that our way of knowing is itself the shape our love takes. Everything that the indifferent call “the past” therefore remains something still to come, to the extent that we love it. Our love is the very source of the future, because it gives the future life. But we must have the courage to love.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
Chapter II Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
1. The central idea of Imami Shiism
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

Let us begin with a broad view of the central ideas of Shiite thought and spiritual life. What I sketch here will be developed more fully in later chapters. Elsewhere I have described the history of Twelver Shiism in terms of four major periods, so I will only recall them briefly here.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

The first period is that of the Imams themselves. It begins with the First Imam, Ali ibn Abi Talib (died 40 AH/661 CE), the Prophet's trusted companion and guardian of his secrets. Shiite tradition preserves a great many conversations and sayings that bear witness to this role. The period ends in 329 AH/940 CE, the year that marks the beginning of the Twelfth Imam's Great Occultation.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

This was also the year in which Muhammad ibn Yaqub Kulayni died. He had been head of the Shiite community in Ray—ancient Rhages, near present-day Tehran—before moving to Baghdad. There he spent twenty years gathering thousands of hadith, reports handed down about religious teachings and events. He drew directly on their transmitters, including the final two representatives (na'ib) of the Twelfth Imam. His work forms the earliest systematic collection of Shiite traditions still known to us.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

Older and more limited collections had already been made. Kulayni could consult some of them, and a few have survived. But persecution caused enormous losses in the Shiite literature of the early centuries, leaving us with many works whose titles are all that remain. Every hadith, as we know, is traced back to one of the Imams through a sequence of witnesses known as its chain of transmission, or isnad.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

The second period runs from Kulayni to the major Twelver Shiite thinker Nasir al-Din Tusi (died 672 AH/1274 CE), who also had dealings with the Seven-Imam, or Ismaili, branch of Shiism. This was above all the age in which scholars compiled the great collections of Shiite traditions, wrote studies devoted to particular questions, and produced major tafsir works—commentaries on the Qur'an.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

The third period extends from Tusi, around the time of the Mongol invasions, to the Safavid revival at the beginning of the sixteenth century. We will return to it in Book IV, particularly through the work of Haydar Amoli, to whom this book owes a special debt.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

The fourth period begins with the Safavid revival. It includes what I have elsewhere called the School of Isfahan, dominated by such figures as Mir Damad and his students (see Book V). It also takes in the Qajar era (see Book VI) and the thinkers who still represent the traditional schools in my own time. Only those who come after us will be able to say when a fifth period began, and in what sense it deserves the name.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

With that brief history in mind, let us turn to the defining features of Shiism. The word shia refers to those Muslims who follow the teaching of the Imams and show them a special devotion. They look to the Imams not only for the ordinary practice of Islam but also for its deepest philosophical teachings and for guidance in understanding the spiritual meaning of the Qur'an.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

The Arabic word tashayyu' means to profess Shiism, while tasannun means to profess Sunni Islam. The latter comes from sunna, meaning tradition. Shiites, of course, also use the word sunna. For them, however, it embraces the full body of transmitted teachings attributed to the Twelve Imams.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

The central distinction can be stated as follows. Sunni Islam teaches that the Prophet Muhammad (died 11 AH/632 CE) brought the cycle of prophecy to an end and revealed the final religious Law, the final sharia. According to the Prophet's own declaration, no prophet and no new revealed Law would follow him. He is the “Seal of Prophecy” (khatim al-nubuwwa), the “Seal of the Prophets” (khatim al-anbiya). On this understanding, the history of divine revelation has reached its conclusion. Generation after generation, Muslims look back to that final point in the past when the sequence of revelations came to a close.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

Shiism also accepts Muhammad as the Seal of Prophecy. But it does not regard humanity's religious history as finished. Here we come to the distinctive Shiite understanding of prophecy, which we will explore in Chapter VI. For the end of the “cycle of prophecy” (da'irat al-nubuwwa) is also the beginning of another cycle: the cycle of spiritual initiation, or walayat.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

The word walayat carries the meaning of friendship; the Persian word is dusti. On one side, it refers to the love and devotion that followers feel for the Imams. On the other, it refers to the love and preference that God has shown the Imams from before the beginning of time, setting them apart as God's Friends, those who are close to God and beloved by God (awliya Allah).
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

Once there are no more prophets (nabi), the title “Friends of God” applies to those who guide their followers—their own “friends”—into the true meaning of the prophetic revelations. In the strict Twelver Shiite sense, this title belongs above all to the Twelve Imams and only secondarily to their followers. Sunni Islam, particularly Sunni Sufism, applies it more widely.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

The cycle of walayat opened when the cycle of prophecy closed. Just as Muhammad embodied the “Seal of universal Prophecy,” so the First Imam embodied the “Seal of universal walayat.” The “Seal of Muhammadan walayat,” however, will be revealed only when the whole cycle of walayat reaches its conclusion: at the appearance of the Twelfth Imam. We will develop these ideas further in Chapters VI and VII of Book I, and again in Book VII.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

The cycle of walayat is the gradual initiation of humanity into the inward, spiritual meaning (batin) of divine revelation. When the Seal of Muhammadan walayat appears, all these hidden meanings will be disclosed. That will be the reign of religion lived entirely in spirit and truth. The Seal will be the final Imam, the Twelfth, returning into the present as the Imam who announces the Resurrection (Qa'im al-Qiyamat).
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

So when a Shiite believer looks back to the Prophet, the Seal of prophetic revelation, that believer also looks towards the figure whom the Prophet himself announced as a descendant, another form of himself: the future Seal of walayat. By accepting the message of the final Prophet, the Imam's followers are not imprisoned in a past that has been closed and sealed. They also look forward, carried by the hidden movement of an ongoing spiritual prophecy, towards the one who will come.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

What this future figure will disclose is not a new Law or a new sharia. It is the inward, hidden meaning of all the revelations given to humanity, which will thereby be transformed and brought into a new light. The way of experiencing religious life is therefore fundamentally different in Shiism and Sunnism.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

Twelver Shiism is also known as Imamism. As we have already seen, the Arabic word Imam originally means “one who stands in front.” The Imam is the spiritual guide. In Iran, the Persian word pishva is also widely used, followed by a number to identify each of the Twelve: pishva-ye yakom, the First Imam; pishva-ye dowom, the Second Imam; and so on.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

In the specifically Shiite sense, the title belongs to the Twelve: Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Prophet's cousin and the first Imam, and eleven descendants of the Prophet through his daughter Fatima (al-Zahra, “the Radiant One”) and Ali. The idea of an Imam as both guide and initiator is inseparable from the idea of Shiism as a path to the deeper knowledge of Islam. The Imam is a guide (hadi) precisely because God has guided him (mahdi).
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

All Twelve Imams can therefore be described as both guided and guiding. Together they form a complete spiritual whole, a pleroma, and share one and the same essential reality (haqiqa, the Greek ousia).
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

The Twelve Imams lead their followers towards the hidden, inward meaning (batin) of the revelation proclaimed by the Prophet. Their teachings form a vast body of tradition, and from the time of the final Prophet until the return of the Hidden Imam they remain the source of a spiritual inheritance that cannot be improvised or reconstructed through logical arguments alone. Their persons, understood as supernatural intermediaries, also remain the focus of their followers' devotion.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

This, in a few words, is what lies at the heart of Shiism. It gives rise to a characteristic way of thinking, a philosophy that calls itself prophetic philosophy (hikmat nabawiya). This is Shiism's distinctive and indispensable contribution to Islam. Sunni thinkers, in general, have not understood this dimension, and it has been just as little recognised in the West. Some in the West, he suggests, have found it easier to admire the prestige of majority Sunni Islam and avoid questions that might disturb their own assumptions. My Shiite friends in Iran have often asked me what lies behind this bias, which they find so strange.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
2. Prophetic philosophy and religion as spiritual initiation
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

This “prophetic philosophy” is, in a sense, what is at stake in Shiism's spiritual struggle on several fronts. Whether Shiism remains true to itself depends on the outcome. For too long, scholars have taken for granted a conventional picture in which Islamic thought and spiritual life appear in three forms: Sufism; the philosophers described as followers of Greek thought; and kalam, usually called Islamic scholastic theology, although it is more accurately a form of argument devoted to defending religious belief.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

But some forms of Sufism reject philosophy and books, while others have created an extraordinary account of the nature of reality, drawing their central themes from the Islamic search for inner knowledge. Likewise, some philosophers reject Sufism, while others embrace it. Then there are the scholars of kalam, the mutakallimun, who generally have no more sympathy for the Sufis and philosophers than those groups have for them.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

Complex as this picture already is, it remains misleading because something essential is missing: Shiite prophetic philosophy. Its method is less a matter of debating abstract ideas than of interpreting and revealing meaning. Instead of building arguments from logical abstractions, it seeks to uncover what lies hidden (batin) beneath what is outwardly visible (zahir), and to recognise how that inner meaning echoes through different levels of reality.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

When Suhrawardi's Ishraq—his “Eastern wisdom,” or philosophy of illumination (see Books II and V)—had become firmly connected with Shiite thought, Iranian writers often described the relationship in a striking way. They said that Ishraq stands in relation to abstract philosophy as Sufism stands in relation to kalam. That comparison alone tells us a great deal about how these different approaches were understood.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

A prophetic philosophy begins with the fact of prophecy. In its understanding of knowledge and the different levels of knowledge, it places prophetic knowledge—the various forms of sacred knowledge—at the summit. That is because its whole account of knowledge grows out of its understanding of prophecy (see Chapter VI below). Its source lies in the teachings handed down from the holy Imams, teachings that often explain the allusions found in a Qur'anic verse. Historically, I do not believe we can trace this kind of thought to any earlier Islamic sources. It even helps explain the structure and language of philosophical systems that have usually been studied on their own.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
We can understand, for example, why al-Farabi, Avicenna, and Suhrawardi all place prophetic knowledge at the highest level of what human beings can know.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

This kind of philosophy naturally belongs to a religion founded on prophecy, such as Islam. Such a religion centres not on the idea that God enters history through a divine incarnation, but on a message given to humanity by a God who always remains beyond the world. God inspires chosen people to communicate that message. If we want to understand the place of philosophy in Islam, and the kind of spiritual life that can grow alongside it, we must look for the setting in which philosophical reflection truly belongs, rather than one where it feels out of place or is rejected. What, then, is the human situation that this philosophy, by its very origins, has to address?
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

The Islamic understanding of human beings and their destiny allows for events that are entirely real without belonging to what we ordinarily call history: events that can be placed on a timeline and documented through material records. This understanding also recognizes events of sacred history beyond ordinary time. They are not events that come after history, but events that reach across and beyond it.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

Just because they are not historical in the usual sense does not mean they are myths in the usual sense either. The ability to recognize reality in this space between myth and recorded history exposes the limits of certain attempts to explain religion through social psychology. Such explanations often begin by assuming that anything must be either myth or history—and that no third possibility exists.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

For Islamic spiritual thought, the central event of this history beyond time is recalled in Qur'an 7:171. God asks the spirits of all human beings, before they have taken bodily form on earth: A-lastu bi-rabbikum?—“Am I not your Lord?” Everyone answers yes.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

Yet, according to the thinkers we are studying, that shared answer conceals many differences, because each person also chose, before entering this world, the destiny they would follow here. This “prologue in heaven” is a central point of reference for Islamic spirituality, although different writers understand it at different depths.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

For Ibn Arabi (d. 638 AH/1240 CE), God was, before the beginning of time, both the one who asked the question and the one who answered it. For Ruzbihan of Shiraz (d. 606/1209; see Book III below), the vision established a bond of love with the eternal Witness (shahid-e qidam), who is at once the one who contemplates and the one contemplated. When human spirits entered their earthly bodies, the love they had known before that passing condition of existence led them to cry out with Moses: “Show Yourself to me.”
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

The mystic thus finds a personal Mount Sinai: the place where God will become manifest to that person. For those who seek inner meanings generally, and for Shiite thinkers especially, the verse clearly points to souls existing before their earthly lives, however that earlier existence is understood. This may explain the distinctly Platonic flavour of the statement of faith drawn up by Shaykh Saduq Ibn Babuyeh (d. 381/991), one of the earliest and most important Shiite scholars. For Muslims more broadly, the verse means that human beings are answerable for a mysterious covenant made with God by God's own will.
